title: Prefixes 小 and 第
explanation: 第 goes before a number to make an order word: 第一 is first, 第二 is second. 小 goes before a surname to make a friendly name for someone younger or close to you, like 小王. When a noun follows 第 + number, you usually still need a measure word: 第一个人.

examples.zh: 今天是我上班的第一天。
examples.py: Jīntiān shì wǒ shàngbān de dì-yī tiān.
examples.en: Today is my first day at work.

examples.py: Xiǎo Wáng shì wǒ de tóngxué.

title: Suffixes 们 and 边
explanation: 们 after a pronoun or a word for people makes it plural: 我们, 同学们. 边 after a direction word makes a place word: 这边, 外边. Don't add 们 when there's already a number: say 三个学生, not 三个学生们.

title: Location words: 上, 下, 里, 外, 前, 后
explanation: These words go after a noun to show where something is: 桌子上 is on the table, 房间里 is in the room. The noun comes first and the location word comes after, which is the opposite of English.

examples.en: The book is on the table.

examples.py: Xuéxiào qiánbian yǒu yí gè shāngdiàn.
examples.en: There's a shop in front of the school.

title: Can: 会 and 能
explanation: 会 means you can do something because you learned how, like speaking a language. 能 means you are able to, or it's possible, in a certain situation. Both go before the verb, and the negatives are 不会 and 不能.

examples.zh: 我生病了，今天不能去上课。
examples.py: Wǒ shēngbìng le, jīntiān bù néng qù shàngkè.
examples.en: I'm sick, so I can't go to class today.

title: Want to: 想 and 要
explanation: Both go before a verb to say what you want to do. 想 is softer, like 'would like to', and 要 is stronger, often meaning 'going to' or 'need to'. To say you don't want to, use 不想, because 不要 means 'don't' as an order.

examples.en: I'd like to drink some tea.
Tomorrow I'm going to the hospital.

title: May, can: 可以
explanation: 可以 means 'can' in the sense of being allowed. Put it before the verb. Use 可以……吗？ to ask for permission, and 不可以 or 不能 to say no.

examples.py: Nǐ kěyǐ kàn wǒ de shū.

point: 看病、睡觉、说话、上课、下课、上班、下班、生病
title: Separable verbs like 睡觉 and 上课
explanation: These verbs are really a verb plus its own object, like 睡 + 觉. Other words can go in the middle: 上了两个小时的课. Because they already have an object, they can't take another one after them: say 和他说话, not 说话他.

examples.zh: 今天我们上了两个小时的课。
examples.py: Jīntiān wǒmen shàng le liǎng gè xiǎoshí de kè.
examples.en: We had two hours of class today.
I'd like to talk with you.

point: 多、多少、几、哪、哪儿、哪里、哪些、什么、谁、怎么、怎么样
title: Question words
explanation: A question word sits in the same place the answer would go: 你是谁？ 我是他哥哥。 Don't add 吗 to a question that already has a question word. 几 is for small numbers, usually under ten, and 多少 is for any number.

examples.py: Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?
examples.en: How many people are there in your family?

point: 我、你、您、他、她、我们、你们、他们、她们、它、它们、大家
title: Personal pronouns
explanation: 我 is I, 你 is you, 他 is he, 她 is she and 它 is it. Add 们 to make them plural. 您 is a polite 'you' for older people or people you don't know well, and 大家 means everyone.

examples.zh: 大家好，我是你们的老师。
examples.py: Dàjiā hǎo, wǒ shì nǐmen de lǎoshī.
Nín hǎo! Tāmen shì wǒ de péngyou.

point: 这、那、这儿、那儿、这里、那里、这些、那些、有的、这个、那个、有些
title: This and that: 这, 那 and friends
explanation: 这 means this (near) and 那 means that (far). Before a noun you usually need a measure word: 这个人, 那本书. 这儿 and 这里 mean here, 那儿 and 那里 mean there, and 有的 or 有些 mean some.

examples.zh: 有的同学在这儿，有的在那儿。
examples.py: Yǒude tóngxué zài zhèr, yǒude zài nàr.
examples.en: Some classmates are here, and some are over there.

point: 一、二/两、三、四、五、六、七、八、九、零、十、百、半、千
title: Numbers, and 二 vs 两
explanation: Numbers build up simply: 十一 is 11, 二十 is 20, 一百 is 100. Before a measure word, use 两 instead of 二: 两个人, not 二个人. 半 means half, so 一个半小时 is an hour and a half.

examples.py: Wǒ xué le yì nián bàn Hànyǔ.
examples.en: I studied Chinese for a year and a half.

point: （1）专用名量词：本、个、家、口、块、件、只、元
title: Measure words for nouns
explanation: Between a number (or 这/那) and a noun, Chinese needs a measure word. 个 is the general one, 本 is for books, 件 for clothes, 只 for many animals, 口 for family members, 家 for shops and companies, and 块 or 元 for money.

examples.py: Wǒ mǎi le sān běn shū.
Wǒ jiā yǒu yì zhī māo.
examples.en: We have a cat at home.

title: Containers as measure words: 杯
explanation: Some container nouns can work as measure words. 一杯水 is a glass of water and 两杯茶 is two cups of tea. Put the number before 杯 and the drink after it.

examples.py: Wǒ xiǎng hē yì bēi chá.
examples.en: I'd like a cup of tea.

examples.py: Qǐng gěi wǒ liǎng bēi shuǐ.

title: Time words: 日, 号, 岁, 点, 分, 年, 天
explanation: 日 and 号 are the day of the month, 岁 is years of age, 点 is o'clock, 分 is minutes, and 年 and 天 are years and days. 年 and 天 go straight after the number with no 个: 三天, not 三个天.

examples.py: Wǒ zài Zhōngguó zhù le sān nián.
examples.en: I lived in China for three years.

title: How much: 很, 非常, 太, 真, 有点儿
explanation: These go before an adjective to say how much. 很 is very, 非常 is extremely, 太 is too (often with 了 at the end), and 真 is really. 有一点儿 means a bit and is usually for something you don't like.
pattern: Subject + 很/非常/太/真/有点儿 + adjective

examples.py: Zhè jiàn yīfu yǒu yìdiǎnr guì.
examples.en: This piece of clothing is a bit expensive.

title: All, both: 都
explanation: 都 means all or both. It goes before the verb, and the people or things it covers come before it. Say 我们都是学生, not 都我们是学生.

examples.py: Bàba māma dōu xǐhuan hē chá.
examples.en: Mum and Dad both like drinking tea.

title: Doing right now: 在 and 正在
explanation: 在 or 正在 before a verb means the action is going on right now. 正在 puts a bit more stress on 'right at this moment'. You can add 呢 at the end too.

examples.en: He's on the phone right now.

title: Again: 再
explanation: 再 before a verb means again or once more, for something that hasn't happened yet. It's common in requests and plans: 请再写一个. For something that already happened again, Chinese uses 又 instead.

title: Also: 也 and 还
explanation: 也 means also or too. It goes after the subject and before the verb, never at the end like English 'too'. 还 adds one more thing, like 'and also'.

examples.zh: 我买了苹果，还买了牛奶。
examples.py: Wǒ mǎi le píngguǒ, hái mǎi le niúnǎi.
examples.en: I bought apples, and some milk as well.

title: Saying no: 不, 没(有), 不要
explanation: 不 is for the present, the future, habits and adjectives: 我不去. 没 or 没有 is for things that didn't happen and for the verb 有: 我昨天没去. 不要 tells someone not to do something, and you never say 不有.

examples.zh: 我昨天没有去，今天也不想去。
examples.py: Wǒ zuótiān méiyǒu qù, jīntiān yě bù xiǎng qù.
examples.en: I didn't go yesterday, and I don't want to go today either.

title: At, in: 在 + place
explanation: 在 + place goes before the verb to say where something happens: 我在家吃饭. English puts the place at the end of the sentence, but Chinese puts it before the verb.

title: With and to: 和 and 对
explanation: 和 + person before a verb means doing something with that person: 我和朋友去. 对 + person means 'to' or 'toward' someone, as in 对我很好, good to me. Both go before the verb.

examples.en: I'm going to the supermarket with Mum.
Our teacher is very good to us.

title: And: 和
explanation: 和 joins two nouns or pronouns: 我和你, 面包和牛奶. Unlike English 'and', it doesn't join two whole sentences.

examples.zh: 我有一个哥哥和一个妹妹。
examples.py: Wǒ yǒu yí gè gēge hé yí gè mèimei.
examples.en: I have an older brother and a younger sister.

examples.py: Wǒ mǎi le miànbāo hé niúnǎi.

title: The particle 的
explanation: 的 links a describing word to a noun, a bit like 's in English: 我的书, 漂亮的衣服. With close family or your own group you can drop it: 我妈妈, 我们学校.

examples.zh: 她买了一件很漂亮的衣服。
examples.py: Tā mǎi le yí jiàn hěn piàoliang de yīfu.
examples.en: She bought a really pretty piece of clothing.

title: Action done: 了 after the verb
explanation: 了 right after a verb shows the action is done. It's most common when the object has a number or describer: 我买了三本书. In the negative you use 没 and drop 了: 我没买.

examples.py: Wǒ chī le liǎng gè bāozi.
Zuótiān wǒ kàn le yí gè diànyǐng.

title: Sentence-end particles: 吗, 吧, 了, 呢
explanation: 吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question. 吧 makes a suggestion or checks a guess, and 了 at the end shows a change. 呢 can ask 'what about...?' (你呢？), ask where something is, or show an action is going on.

title: Hello on the phone: 喂
explanation: 喂 is what you say when you answer or start a phone call, like 'hello?'. On the phone it's usually said wéi. Said as wèi to get a stranger's attention, it can sound rude.

examples.en: Hello, may I ask who's calling?

title: Joined phrases: A and B
explanation: A joined phrase puts two or more words of the same kind side by side as equals, like 爸爸妈妈 or 老师和学生. The whole thing works as one unit in the sentence, often followed by 都.

examples.py: Lǎoshī hé xuésheng dōu lái le.
examples.en: The teacher and the students have all come.
Mum and Dad are both at home.

title: Describer + main word phrases
explanation: In Chinese the describing part always comes before the word it describes: 新书 is a new book, 非常好 is very good. This works for nouns and for verbs and adjectives.

examples.py: Zhè shì yì běn xīn shū.

title: Verb + object phrases
explanation: The object comes after the verb, as in English: 看电影, 学汉语. Many daily activities are said as a verb with a general object, like 吃饭 for eating a meal.

title: Subject + predicate phrases
explanation: A small subject + predicate unit can sit inside a bigger sentence, often after verbs like 知道 or 觉得: 我知道他是医生. The inside part keeps its normal word order.

examples.py: Wǒ juéde zhège cài hěn hǎochī.
examples.en: I think this dish is really good.

title: Number + measure word phrases
explanation: A number plus a measure word makes a phrase like 三个 or 两本. It usually goes before a noun, but it can stand on its own when everyone knows what you mean: 我要两个.

title: Preposition phrases
explanation: A preposition and its object, like 在家 or 和朋友, make one phrase. It normally goes before the main verb, not after it.

examples.en: I'm going to the bookshop with a friend.

title: Place phrases: noun + location word
explanation: A noun plus a location word, like 桌子上 or 房间里, makes a place phrase. It often follows 在, and it can also start a sentence before 有.

examples.py: Wǒ de shǒujī zài zhuōzi shang.
examples.en: My phone is on the table.

point: 名词、代词或名词性短语作主语
title: The subject
explanation: The subject is who or what the sentence is about. It's usually a noun, a pronoun or a noun phrase, and it comes first, before the verb.

point: 名词、代词、数词或数量短语作谓语
title: Nouns and numbers as the predicate
explanation: For dates, ages and prices, Chinese can skip 是 and use a noun or number phrase right after the subject: 今天星期三. In the negative you have to bring 是 back: 今天不是星期三.

point: 动词或动词性短语、形容词或形容词性短语作谓语
title: Verbs and adjectives as the predicate
explanation: Most predicates are a verb phrase like 看电视 or an adjective phrase like 很好. Adjectives don't need 是: say 她很漂亮, not 她是漂亮.

examples.en: My little brother is watching TV.

point: 名词、代词或名词性短语作宾语
title: The object
explanation: The object comes after the verb and is usually a noun, a pronoun or a noun phrase. It can be long, like 一本新书, and still sits after the verb.

examples.py: Wǒ xiǎng mǎi yì běn xīn shū.
examples.en: I want to buy a new book.

point: 名词性词语、形容词性短语、数量短语作定语
title: Words that describe a noun
explanation: Describing words go in front of the noun. This can be a noun (中国菜), an adjective phrase (很大的房间) or a number + measure word (三本书). When the describer is a phrase like 很大, add 的 before the noun.

examples.zh: 他家有一个很大的房间。
examples.py: Tā jiā yǒu yí gè hěn dà de fángjiān.
examples.en: His home has a really big room.

point: 副词、形容词作状语表示时间、处所的词语作状语
title: Words before the verb: when, where, how
explanation: Words that say when, where or how an action happens go before the verb: 明天, 在学校, 都. Time words can go before or after the subject, but not at the end of the sentence as in English.

title: How many times: verb + 一下
explanation: A count word after the verb says how many times, or how briefly, you do it. 一下 after a verb makes it short and casual, like 'have a quick look' for 看一下. It also makes requests sound softer.

examples.en: I'd like to rest for a bit.
Could you come here for a moment?

title: Sentences with a verb
explanation: The most common sentence is subject + verb (+ object): 我去商店. Words for time, place or manner go between the subject and the verb.

title: Sentences with an adjective
explanation: Chinese adjectives work like verbs, so you don't need 是. A plain adjective usually takes 很, even when you don't mean 'very'. Without 很 it can sound like you're comparing.

title: Sentences with a noun as predicate
explanation: For dates, ages, prices and times you can put a noun phrase right after the subject with no verb: 明天十号. To say no, use 不是: 明天不是十号.

title: Sentences with no subject
explanation: Some sentences have no subject at all and are still complete. This is common for weather (下雨了), requests (请坐) and short replies.

title: Statements
explanation: A statement tells a fact and ends with a full stop. The basic order is subject + verb + object. To make it negative, put 不 or 没 before the verb.

title: Yes/no questions with 吗
explanation: Add 吗 to the end of a statement to make a yes/no question, and keep the word order the same. To answer, repeat the verb: 是 or 不是, 喜欢 or 不喜欢.

title: Questions with a question word
explanation: Put a question word like 什么, 谁 or 哪儿 where the answer would go. The rest of the sentence stays in normal order, and you don't add 吗.

title: Verb-not-verb questions
explanation: Say the verb or adjective twice with 不 in the middle: 去不去, 好吃不好吃. For 有, use 有没有. Don't add 吗 to this kind of question.

examples.en: Do you have an older brother?
Is this dish good or not?

title: Requests and commands
explanation: Requests and commands usually drop the subject. 请 at the start makes them polite, and 不要 tells someone not to do something. 吧 at the end softens it.

title: Exclamations
explanation: Exclamations show strong feeling and end with ！. Two easy forms are 太 + adjective + 了 and 真 + adjective.
pattern: 太 + adjective + 了！ / 真 + adjective！

title: A 是 B
explanation: A 是 B says that A is B, or that A belongs to the kind B: 我是学生. The negative is 不是. Use 是 to link nouns, not before adjectives.

examples.py: Zhè bú shì wǒ de shǒujī.

title: Having: A 有 B
explanation: A 有 B means A has B. The negative is always 没有, never 不有.

title: What's at a place: place + 是 + noun
explanation: Place + 是 + noun tells you what is at that place, when you're naming the thing: 前边是学校. The place comes first. Compare 有, which just says that something is there.

examples.py: Wǒ jiā qiánbian shì yí gè shāngdiàn.
examples.en: In front of my home is a shop.

examples.py: Zhuōzi shang shì wǒ de shū.
examples.en: Those are my books on the table.

title: There is: place + 有 + number + noun
explanation: To say 'there is' or 'there are', start with the place, then 有, then the number + measure word + noun. Don't put 在 in front of the place in this pattern.
pattern: Place + 有 + number + measure word + Noun

examples.py: Zhuōzi shang yǒu yì běn shū.
examples.en: There's a book on the table.

examples.py: Fángjiān li yǒu liǎng gè xuésheng.
examples.en: There are two students in the room.

point: （1）前后动作先后发生，后一动作是前一动作的目的
title: Going somewhere to do something
explanation: Two verb phrases can follow each other with nothing in between. In 去/来 + place + verb, the second action is the reason for going: 我去商店买东西. You don't need a word for 'to'.
pattern: Subject + 去/来 + place + Verb + Object

examples.en: I'm going to the shop to buy fruit.
He came to China to learn Chinese.

point: （2）前一动作是后一动作的方式
title: How you do it: 坐 + vehicle + 去
explanation: The first verb phrase shows how the second action is done. A common case is 坐 + vehicle + 去/来: 我坐飞机去. The way of travel comes before 去, not after.
pattern: Subject + 坐 + vehicle + 去/来 + place

examples.en: I'm taking a taxi to the hospital.

title: Two objects: give someone something
explanation: Some verbs, like 给 and 问, can take two objects. The person comes first and the thing second: 我给你一本书.

examples.py: Wǒ gěi nǐ yí gè píngguǒ.
Wǒ wèn lǎoshī yí gè wèntí.
examples.en: I asked the teacher a question.

title: Two clauses with no linking word
explanation: Two short clauses can just sit side by side with a comma. The link, like 'so' or 'but', is clear from the meaning, so Chinese often leaves it out.

examples.py: Wǒ shēngbìng le, jīntiān bú shàngbān.
examples.en: I'm sick, so I'm not going to work today.

examples.py: Tā hē chá, wǒ hē niúnǎi.
examples.en: He drinks tea and I drink milk.

title: ……，也……: and also
explanation: The second clause uses 也 to add something similar. 也 goes after the subject and before the verb. If the subject is the same, you can drop it in the second clause.

examples.py: Wǒ shì xuésheng, tā yě shì xuésheng.
examples.en: I'm a student, and so is he.

examples.py: Wǒ xǐhuan māo, yě xǐhuan gǒu.
examples.en: I like cats, and I like dogs too.

title: ……，还……: and on top of that
explanation: 还 in the second clause adds one more thing, like 'and also'. It goes before the verb, and the subject is usually the same as in the first clause.

examples.zh: 我会说汉语，还会写汉字。
examples.py: Wǒ huì shuō Hànyǔ, hái huì xiě Hànzì.
examples.en: I can speak Chinese, and I can write characters too.

examples.zh: 她买了衣服，还买了一本书。
examples.py: Tā mǎi le yīfu, hái mǎi le yì běn shū.
examples.en: She bought clothes, and a book as well.

title: Finished actions with 了
explanation: 了 right after the verb shows the action is finished. It's often used with a number or describer on the object: 写了三个汉字. To say it didn't happen, use 没 and leave out 了.

examples.py: Wǒ zuótiān mǎi le hěn duō shuǐguǒ.
examples.en: I bought a lot of fruit yesterday.

examples.py: Tā xiě le sān gè Hànzì.

title: Change with 了 at the end
explanation: 了 at the end of a sentence shows something has changed or a new situation has started: 天冷了 means it's got cold. With 不, it means you no longer do something.

examples.zh: 我现在不喜欢喝牛奶了。
examples.py: Wǒ xiànzài bù xǐhuan hē niúnǎi le.
examples.en: I don't like drinking milk anymore.

title: In progress: 在/正在 + verb
explanation: Put 在 or 正在 before the verb to show an action is happening now. The object follows the verb as usual.

title: In progress: 在/正在 + verb + 呢
explanation: Adding 呢 at the end of an 在 or 正在 sentence makes it sound more natural and spoken. The meaning stays 'is doing right now'.
pattern: Subject + 在/正在 + Verb + Object + 呢

title: In progress: just 呢
explanation: 呢 at the end of a sentence can show an action is going on even without 在. It's common in casual speech.

title: Talking about money
explanation: In speech people say 块 for yuan, and in writing 元. 钱 can follow 块 but is often dropped. A price like 3.50 is said 三块五, leaving off the last unit.

examples.py: Yí gè miànbāo bā kuài qián.
examples.en: A loaf of bread is eight yuan.

title: First, second: 第 + number
explanation: Put 第 before a number to make an order word: 第一, 第二, 第三. Add a measure word before a noun: 第一个学生.

examples.py: Tā shì dì-yī gè lái de.
examples.en: He was the first one to arrive.

title: Dates and days of the week
explanation: Chinese dates go from big to small: year, month, day, then weekday. In speech the day is usually 号, and in writing 日. Weekdays are 星期 + a number, except Sunday, which is 星期天 or 星期日.
pattern: year + 月 + 号/日 + 星期

examples.py: Jīntiān shì shí yuè yī hào.

title: Telling the time
explanation: Use 点 for o'clock and 分 for minutes: 八点十分 is 8:10. 半 means half past, so 三点半 is 3:30. Clock time goes before the verb: 我七点起床.
pattern: Number + 点 (+ number + 分 / 半)

examples.en: I get up at seven in the morning.
